entry.title: OpenAI Cuts Off Adobe, Others From Advertising Some Competing AI Products in ChatGPT
entry.content:
OpenAI has told some business partners that it will no longer accept advertising in ChatGPT for image- and audio-generating products—which compete with its own features.

The change, which hasn’t been previously reported or reflected in its published ads policy, blindsided existing advertisers such as Adobe, which sells such products. And if extended to other competing products, the new policy could narrow OpenAI’s potential ad revenue. OpenAI has given investors aggressive projections for ad growth, which it sees as a key way to make money off its large audience of people who don’t pay for the service.

entry.title: OpenAI Math Result Stokes Data-Sharing Concerns
entry.content:
In case you missed it: we got an eye-catching X post on Tuesday night from Evan Hubinger, a leader of Anthropic's alignment efforts. Responding to the resignation announcement of an Anthropic employee who warned that AI companies aren’t doing enough to ensure AI won't kill humanity, Hubinger wrote that the employee is “correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade.” Hubinger added that he was worried about future AI models, not those currently available, but still, yikes!

Meanwhile, our colleague Jyoti sizes up the significance of Meta’s new personal AI agent, Muse, unveiled on Tuesday. That’s below. But before we get to that:

This may go down as the year the AI industry got a crash course in mathematics. Breakthroughs in AI models have yielded announcements on such arcane subjects as the “Erdős unit distance problem” and the “Jacobian Conjecture,” which observers have watched as an indicator of AI progress in other domains.

The latest announcement, OpenAI's claim on Tuesday that it had solved the vexing “Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem,” has drawn attention for another reason: questions over whether its math-genius models may have gained an edge by incorporating data from two human mathematicians that had used OpenAI's Codex in their work on the same problem. Those questions fed into concerns about the possibility of AI companies learning from customers’ use of their AI models to develop competing products.

entry.title: Confusion Reigns Over White House’s AI Whitelist
entry.content:
It may be one of the hottest tickets in corporate America right now: membership in the “trusted partner” program that allows companies to get access to the most advanced AI models before they’re released to the public. There’s just one problem: no one outside of the Trump administration has a clear idea how to get on that list.

As laid out in the administration’s executive order in early June, which established a voluntary testing framework for frontier AI models, these “trusted partners”— including banks, cybersecurity firms and power utilities—would use their access to sniff out potential vulnerabilities in their computer systems exposed by the new AI models.

entry.title: China Curbs Humanoid IPOs After Unitree’s Volatile Debut
entry.content:
Chinese regulators are tightening the approval for humanoid startups seeking to go public after a volatile debut by industry leader Unitree Robotics, as they aim to cool down a sizzling sector rife with copycats but little real technological breakthroughs.

The Chinese Securities Regulatory Commission recently gave its informal “window guidance” to some investment banks and investment firms that it is raising the bar for granting approval of humanoid IPOs, according to people with knowledge of the matter. Companies must demonstrate they can generate recurring revenue, are on a path to narrow their losses or achieve real innovation before approvals can be considered, the people added.

entry.title: Gimlet's Three-Tranche Deal Reveals AI Funding Frenzy
entry.content:
Gimlet Labs said late last week it had raised $300 million at a valuation of about $3 billion, in a round led by new investor Andreessen Horowitz. Today we have unreported details on how that round, which boosted its valuation by a whopping 16 times from its last PitchBook valuation, came together.

The three-year-old startup, which helps AI developers run models using different AI chips simultaneously, raised the round after the company’s executives told some potential investors that based on signed contracts, OpenAI was likely to spend more than $100 million a year on its services, according to a person familiar with the company. Such outlays, if they transpire, would be significant given it just emerged from stealth in October. 

This windfall would be in the future, however. “We have explored possibilities with Gimlet but we are not a paying customer,” said an OpenAI spokesperson.

entry.title: Why Price Cuts May Rattle Anthropic's IPO Pitch
entry.content:
Anthropic’s IPO paperwork is expected to become public sometime soon. But it was OpenAI finance chief Sarah Friar who drew a standing-room-only crowd Tuesday at San Francisco’s Palace Hotel, as Goldman Sachs kicked off its annual Communacopia + Technology conference with a Q&A with Friar. In her talk, Friar made clear how important price has become for determining model popularity—a potential problem for Anthropic, widely seen as the high-end AI provider.

Friar described how a price cut on OpenAI’s GPT 5.6 Luna model led to a tenfold increase in use, my colleague Anita Ramaswamy reported, giving OpenAI the highest market share on OpenRouter, a service developers use to access different models. We wrote in mid-August that Luna had generated more than twice the token usage of Anthropic’s Opus 5 and Sonnet 5 models on OpenRouter. Judging from Friar’s comments Tuesday, the increase in usage was enough to offset the price cut.

entry.title: Hugging Face Is Making A Big Robotics Push
entry.content:
Nvidia is paying a steep price for Hugging Face, a repository of open source models, primarily for its strategic position in the center of the open source AI world. But it turns out Nvidia is also getting a budding robot business that could help CEO Jensen Huang fulfill the promise of “physical AI.” 

Hugging Face late last month launched Microduck, a small robot that can walk around and learn skills like roller skating or pointing lasers at walls for cats to chase. The company has already sold more than 15,000 ducks, generating over $6 million in sales, despite limited advertising on X and LinkedIn, Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf told me. 

The new robot is part of Hugging Face’s push to sell affordable robots built on open source AI for consumers and developers. That shaped its strategy with its April 2025 acquisition of Pollen Robotics, which previously focused on pricier humanoid robots but shifted to making more affordable, accessible robots after the deal, Wolf explained.

entry.title: How to Use Google Gemini for Market Research and Campaign Planning
entry.content:
For marketers, the start of annual campaign planning is the ultimate blank page.

Even with access to comprehensive product information and results from past campaigns, it can be daunting to begin pulling this data together and finding ways to improve in the year ahead. Often, marketing leaders are overwhelmed with a combination of highly technical product roadmaps and dense spreadsheets detailing last year’s campaign metrics, and it can take days of manual cross-referencing and analysis to simply figure out where to start.

By synthesizing market research, product specs, and historical data, Gemini can help your team map out a data-informed go-to-market strategy.

Step 1: Sketch Out Your Baseline Buyer Personas

To start, you can use Gemini’s vast training data to help you build a detailed profile of your target buyers. You’ll need to give Gemini a rough directional target to make sure these personas are as specific as possible. Jot down your timeline, product category, and high-level audience definition, and then ask Gemini to use this information to help you brainstorm ways to reach these buyers.

Here’s a sample prompt:

I’m a marketing leader conducting analysis in preparation for next year’s [launch]. Define my target audiences [audiences], for my new line of [product]. Include interests, relevant marketing channels, and top trends that drive their consideration and purchase behavior.

Gemini will return a set of potential audience segments based on your inputs. For example, if you’re marketing a high-end technical jacket, results might include the Active Executive Commuter, the Global Business Traveler, and the Tech-Forward Urbanite, with different purchase drivers for each persona.

Step 2: Break Down Your Data Silos

Now that you have your buyer personas sketched out, it’s time to bring in additional information to give Gemini the context it needs to find historical lessons and apply them to your next campaign.


Gather past campaign performance data, corresponding product information, and your own insights on what worked and what went wrong. Sticking with the example of a premium jacket: Perhaps you will note that social media ads underperformed for last year’s line, with brand-aligned messaging about sustainable manufacturing failing to effectively drive purchase intent. Or, you might note that sponsored videos from travel gear creators drove the highest volume of sales.

Be as thorough and as specific as possible. The more information Gemini has about the past, the better it can help you plan for the future.

Step 3: Brainstorm Campaign Messaging

Now that Gemini has information about your product, your buyers, and your past campaigns, it can help you brainstorm ideas for how to conduct your next campaign.

Try this prompt:

Brainstorm value props for my [target audiences] based on features from [Product Requirements Document]. Include a section on campaign learnings from [Campaign Performance].

Gemini will suggest specific value propositions for each buyer persona that it previously outlined. For example, Gemini might note that the Active Executive Commuter is likely to focus on the jacket’s underarm vents, while the Global Business Traveler might care more about the jacket’s hidden pockets.

Use Gemini’s suggestions as a starting point for campaign messaging, rather than treating them like an unchangeable roadmap. While Gemini can spark ideas, your team’s expertise is needed to identify which of these ideas will work in the real world.

Step 4: Execute Your Campaign

After you’ve finalized your broad campaign messaging, you can come back to Gemini for help executing specific tactics. Here are some prompts you might try:

Turn these value propositions into a creative brief for our design team.

Draft three distinct variations of 15-second ad scripts showcasing [Feature X] for our target audience.

Outline a landing page wireframe that emphasizes these new value props.

Gemini’s creative brief will bring together information about your existing target audience and messaging angles, creative guardrails and format requirements, and key deliverables. Its ad scripts will offer ideas for specific visuals and voiceover text. And its landing page wireframe will outline a design meant to prioritize clarity and conversion, complete with ideas for headlines, hero image, and call to action.

Here again, you should tweak Gemini’s output, going back and forth in the chat to refine your vision as your campaign planning becomes more concrete. Human intuition will always be part of any successful campaign launch. But when you first use product data and past campaign information to generate initial ideas, you no longer have to start from scratch.
